title: Choosing good use cases
point: The best AI tasks are high volume, low risk and easy to verify, in an area where you are expert enough to judge the output.
definition: A use case is a specific, repeated task you hand to an AI assistant. A good one saves time without creating harm you cannot catch.

objective.text: Choose and justify the two best AI use cases from a list of six team tasks, using volume, risk, ease of checking and your own expertise.

misconceptions.claim: The hardest tasks are the best place to use AI, because that is where help is needed most.
misconceptions.correction: Hard tasks are often the ones you cannot check. Start with routine tasks you understand well, where you can spot a mistake at a glance.

misconceptions.claim: If the assistant is right most of the time, it is fine for decisions about people.
misconceptions.correction: Hiring, pay, performance and discipline decisions affect people's lives and carry legal duties. A person must make them, whatever the tool's accuracy.

l1: Look for four signs of a good use case: high volume, low risk, easy to verify, and you are the expert who can judge the result.
Poor use cases include final decisions about people, legal or medical advice, and anything you cannot check.
Good examples include first drafts of routine emails, meeting summaries from your own notes, and reformatting a list into a table.
l2: A sales team lists tasks: drafting follow-up emails, summarising call notes, setting discount levels for key accounts, and interpreting a contract clause.
Follow-up emails and call summaries are frequent, low risk and easy for the salesperson to check, so they are good starts.
Discount levels and contract clauses carry financial and legal risk. They need a manager or the legal team, not an assistant.
l3: Score each task by minutes saved per week minus minutes spent checking. A task saving 60 minutes with 10 minutes of checking nets 50 minutes.
A task saving 20 minutes that needs 25 minutes of careful checking loses time, so drop it even if it looks impressive.
Pick the tasks with the highest net saving and the lowest harm if something slips through.
